content.narrative_summary: Bifascicular block refers to ECG evidence of impaired conduction below the AV node in the right and left bundles. Alternating bundle-branch block is present when block in all three fascicles manifests on successive ECGs. Examples include right bundle-branch block with left anterior or posterior fascicular block on different ECGs. Patients with first-degree AV block plus bifascicular block and symptoms have high mortality and substantial incidence of sudden death, though progression to third-degree AV block is slow. No single clinical or laboratory variable, including bifascicular block, reliably predicts future bradyarrhythmia risk. Syncope is common in bifascicular block but not linked to increased sudden death; pacing relieves neurologic symptoms but does not reduce sudden death. Electrophysiological study may guide treatment of inducible ventricular arrhythmias. If syncope cause is uncertain or treatments exacerbate AV block, prophylactic pacing is indicated, especially when syncope may be due to transient third-degree AV block. PR and HV intervals have been studied as predictors of third-degree AV block and sudden death, but correlation with block progression and sudden death is unclear.

section_headings: Recommendations for Pacing After Cardiac Transplantation
2.3. Prevention and Termination of Arrhythmias by Pacing
content.narrative_summary: Conduction system disease progressing to complete AV block in neuromuscular disorders (eg, myotonic dystrophy, Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy) can warrant permanent pacing even in asymptomatic patients with ECG or HV interval abnormalities. In obstructive sleep apnea, atrial tachyarrhythmias and bradycardia occur but atrial overdrive pacing has not been shown effective; nasal continuous positive airway pressure is preferred. Central sleep apnea and Cheyne–Stokes breathing in heart failure may improve with CRT. Cardiac sarcoidosis often involves the AV node and can cause block or life-threatening VT; pacemaker implantation is recommended even if conduction may transiently improve, and immunosuppression with steroids may prevent progression. For arrhythmia termination, pacemakers can terminate re-entrant SVT and VT with programmed stimulation or overdrive, may prevent pause-dependent VT in long-QT syndrome (often with beta-blockers), and ICDs with overdrive suppression should be considered in high-risk patients.

Criteria for implantation in asymptomatic children and adolescents (average heart rate, pauses, structural heart disease, QT interval, exercise tolerance) are described. section_headings: 2.6.7. Importance of Minimizing Unnecessary Ventricular Pacing
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews clinical trial evidence regarding end points for dual-chamber versus ventricular pacing. The Danish study demonstrated improved heart failure status with atrial pacing versus ventricular pacing, but meta-analysis showed no significant difference in new-onset heart failure hospitalization between pacing modes. Studies (MOST, CTOPP) found significantly lower atrial fibrillation incidence with atrial or dual-chamber pacing (hazard ratio 0.80), with benefits emerging by 6 months. Stroke or thromboembolism was reduced in the Danish trial, though meta-analysis did not reach significance. The Danish study also showed reduced overall and cardiovascular mortality with atrial pacing, but pooled data did not confirm mortality benefit. Finally, emerging recognition of deleterious effects of right ventricular pacing has led to recommendations to minimize unnecessary ventricular pacing; more frequent ventricular pacing may negate AV synchrony benefits.

content.narrative_summary: This page reviews evidence supporting implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) therapy for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular tachycardia across multiple disease states. In coronary artery disease, ICDs confer a survival benefit and should follow optimal revascularization when indicated. In nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, ICDs are preferred over antiarrhythmic drugs for survivors of ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy warrants suspicion in young individuals with exertional risk and favors ICD implantation in those resuscitated from arrest. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia/cardiomyopathy, characterized by fibrofatty RV infiltration, shows high rates of appropriate ICD interventions. Genetic arrhythmia syndromes, including long- and short-QT, Brugada, idiopathic VF, and catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, predispose to life-threatening arrhythmias and indicate consideration of ICD therapy.
